questions.stem_markdown: A 17-year-old attends a Sydney adolescent clinic for contraception review and says, "I’m using protection and I don’t think I have an STI, so there isn’t really a sexual health issue even though sex is making me stressed about the relationship." What is the **best response** based on the notes?

options.text: Sexual health is mainly about avoiding pregnancy, so relationship stress is outside its scope
Sexual health includes physical, emotional, mental, and social wellbeing related to sexuality, so relationship-related distress still matters
Sexual health discussions are only relevant once genital symptoms appear
A sexual health review should stop once contraception is reliable
Sexual health in adolescence is mainly a legal issue rather than a wellbeing issue

questions.explanation_markdown: The Louisa notes define **sexual health** as a state of **physical, emotional, mental, and social wellbeing related to sexuality**. This means sexual health is broader than pregnancy or infection alone, so relationship-related distress is still clinically relevant.

why_others_wrong.A: The notes define sexual health more broadly than pregnancy prevention alone.
why_others_wrong.C: The source material does not limit sexual health discussion to symptomatic presentations.
why_others_wrong.D: Reliable protection does not remove the broader emotional, mental, and social aspects of sexual health described in the notes.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes frame sexual health as a wellbeing concept, not mainly as a legal one.

key_takeaways: Sexual health is broader than STI status or pregnancy risk.
Emotional and social wellbeing are part of sexual health in the notes.
Protection alone does not make every sexual health concern disappear.

questions.stem_markdown: A 16-year-old in NSW says her new partner is 17 and worries that any consensual sexual activity would automatically be illegal because the partner is older. What is the **best clinician response** based on the notes?

options.text: Any age difference makes sexual activity unlawful until both people are 18
If both people are 16 or older and both freely consent, sexual intercourse or other sexual acts can be lawful
Sexual activity is lawful only if both families approve of the relationship
At 16, only kissing is lawful but not any other sexual act
Legality depends mainly on how long the relationship has lasted

questions.explanation_markdown: The Louisa notes state that the **age of consent is 16** in NSW and that someone who is **16 years or older** can legally have sexual intercourse or participate in other sexual acts with another person who is **16 years or older**, provided **both freely consent**.

why_others_wrong.A: The notes do not say that any age difference makes the activity unlawful once both people are 16 or older and freely consenting.
why_others_wrong.C: Family approval is not the legal criterion described in the notes.
why_others_wrong.D: The source material does not create a special rule limiting 16-year-olds to kissing only.
why_others_wrong.E: Relationship duration is not the legal test given in the notes.

key_takeaways: The notes frame the NSW age of consent around age 16 and free consent.
A small age difference above 16 is not described as automatically unlawful.
Accurate, calm communication helps adolescents understand the legal framework without unnecessary alarm.

questions.stem_markdown: A school health coordinator sees that teen pregnancy and birth rates have been relatively stable since the 1990s and concludes that sexual health promotion can probably be scaled back because adolescent sexual risk must be falling overall. Which interpretation best fits the notes?

options.text: Yes. Stable teen birth rates prove that STI risk is also falling
Not necessarily. The notes say STIs are rising, and stable teen births may reflect improved sexual education despite contextual changes
Yes. Stable teen birth rates mean that first sexual experience now usually occurs only after monogamy is established
Yes. Stable teen birth rates mean adolescents no longer need protection counselling
Not necessarily, but only because adolescents are no longer sexually active

questions.explanation_markdown: The Louisa notes state that, despite an **increasing gap between first sexual experience and monogamy**, **STIs are on the rise** while **teen pregnancy/births have been stable since the 1990s**, probably reflecting **improved sexual education**. Stable birth rates therefore do not mean sexual health risk has disappeared.

why_others_wrong.A: The notes explicitly state that STIs are on the rise, so stable birth rates do not prove falling STI risk.
why_others_wrong.C: The notes describe the opposite trend: an increasing gap between first sexual experience and monogamy.
why_others_wrong.D: The source material does not support reducing protection counselling on this basis.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes do not say adolescents are no longer sexually active.

key_takeaways: Stable teen birth rates do not mean all sexual health risks are falling.
The notes describe rising STI rates despite stable teen births.
Population trends need careful interpretation rather than simplistic conclusions.

questions.stem_markdown: A 14-year-old asks for help "not making stupid relationship decisions." She has started dating early, spends a lot of time home alone, is missing school, feels bad about herself, and has recently started drinking at parties. According to the notes, what is the **best focus for follow-up**?

options.text: Wait until she reports sexual intercourse before offering sexual health support
Limit follow-up to condom teaching because the other issues are separate from sexual risk
Broaden support to include sexual health counselling plus school engagement, family supervision/relationships, self-esteem and mental health, and other risk behaviours
Focus only on whether her peers are currently sexually active
Reassure her that early dating is not relevant unless there is already an STI or pregnancy

questions.explanation_markdown: The CAH Bible lists predictors of risky sexual behaviour across several domains, including **early dating**, **time home alone**, **poor parental monitoring or family relationships**, **poor school attendance/academic ability**, **low self-efficacy and self-esteem**, **poor mental health**, and **other risky behaviour**. The best follow-up therefore addresses these wider drivers, not contraception alone.

why_others_wrong.A: The notes support earlier preventive work rather than waiting for intercourse to occur.
why_others_wrong.B: The CAH Bible specifically describes multiple psychosocial predictors, so limiting care to condom teaching is too narrow.
why_others_wrong.D: Peers matter, but this option ignores several other note-based drivers already present in the stem.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes identify early dating and associated psychosocial factors as relevant before STI or pregnancy occurs.

key_takeaways: Risky sexual behaviour is shaped by psychosocial context as well as the sexual act itself.
Prevention may need family, school, mental health, and risk-behaviour support together.
Early intervention can be appropriate before intercourse, STI, or pregnancy is reported.

questions.stem_markdown: A 13-year-old says, "I’ve only done oral stuff, not intercourse, so sexual health counselling can wait." Which response best matches the notes?

options.text: That is reasonable because only sexual intercourse predicts later risky sexual behaviour
That is reasonable because non-intercourse behaviours are outside adolescent sexual health
Early dating and non-intercourse sexual behaviours can still signal later risky sexual behaviour, so prevention-focused counselling is appropriate now
Counselling should wait until the adolescent reaches the legal age of consent
Counselling is only needed once pregnancy becomes possible

questions.explanation_markdown: The CAH Bible lists **early dating** and **non-intercourse sexual behaviours** among the predictors of risky sexual behaviour. That means prevention-focused counselling does not need to wait until penile-vaginal intercourse has occurred.

why_others_wrong.A: The notes do not limit risk prediction to intercourse alone.
why_others_wrong.B: Non-intercourse sexual behaviours are specifically relevant in the CAH Bible predictor list.
why_others_wrong.D: The source material does not say clinicians should delay counselling until the age of consent is reached.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes frame sexual health more broadly than pregnancy risk alone.

key_takeaways: Prevention-focused sexual health counselling can be appropriate before intercourse occurs.
Early dating and non-intercourse sexual behaviours are relevant in the notes.
Waiting for a higher-risk event may miss useful early support opportunities.

questions.stem_markdown: A GP writes after a 16-year-old’s first consensual sexual experience, "Future sexual health review is probably less important now because first sex usually coincides with monogamy." According to the notes, which correction is best?

options.text: The notes suggest there is an increasing gap between first sexual experience and monogamy, so clinicians should not assume they occur together
The notes say first sexual experience now usually occurs only after monogamy is established
The notes say first sexual experience and monogamy have become more tightly linked over time
The notes say monogamy is no longer relevant to sexual health at all
The notes say first sexual experience is no longer a meaningful part of adolescent sexual behaviour

questions.explanation_markdown: The Louisa notes state that, due to contextual changes, there is an **increasing gap between first sexual experience and monogamy**. This means clinicians should avoid assuming those two milestones happen together or that risk discussions can automatically narrow after first sex.

why_others_wrong.B: The notes describe the opposite trend rather than saying monogamy is already established first.
why_others_wrong.C: The source material does not say the two milestones have become more tightly linked.
why_others_wrong.D: The notes do not dismiss monogamy as irrelevant; they describe how its timing relative to first sex has changed.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes still discuss first sexual experience as an important part of adolescent sexual behaviour trends.

key_takeaways: The notes describe a widening gap between first sexual experience and monogamy.
Clinicians should avoid assuming first sex means sexual behaviour has become simple or settled.
Trend data can shape more realistic sexual health follow-up.
